screens.title: The SOLID Principles — Part 1
screens.subtitle: Why SRP and OCP make C# code easier to change and extend

narration.text: In this lesson we focus on the first two pillars of SOLID: the Single Responsibility Principle and the Open/Closed Principle. These guidelines are not abstract rules; they are practical habits that reduce risk when software changes. SRP helps you group related behavior so a change to one concern doesn't ripple into unrelated code. OCP helps you add new features by extending the system instead of editing stable, tested code. Together they make code easier to test, reason about, and extend. We'll study concrete C# examples that show common violations — a User class that both stores data and handles persistence and email, and a discount calculator that branches on product categories. Then we will refactor to isolate responsibilities using interfaces and to support new behavior by adding implementations rather than editing existing classes. As you learn, notice a pattern: identify a single reason a class might change, and then ask whether new behavior can be added as a new type rather than by changing existing code. That question is the heart of maintainable design. Ready to explore SRP and OCP with code and guided refactors?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: SRP reduces reasons to change a class. OCP lets you add features by extending with new implementations instead of modifying working code.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › The SOLID Principles — Part 1

The SOLID Principles — Part 1

SRP and OCP are practical tools you will use to keep C# codebases adaptable. This lesson gives examples, refactor patterns, and a small exercise you can apply immediately.

Duration: ~15 minutes
Why SRP

Isolating responsibilities reduces unexpected side effects when requirements change and improves testability.

Why OCP

Extensibility through new implementations prevents edits to tested code, lowering regression risk.

Example
A User class mixed with persistence and email is brittle.
Refactor Pattern
Extract interfaces for persistence and email and orchestrate through a service.
Practice
Refactor a DocumentSaver to accept different savers via an interface.
Concept Map
SRP → OCP → Interfaces → Extensibility
SRP
Single focused responsibilities, easier tests and safer changes.
OCP
Extend with new types, keep core stable.
Explore Key Topics
SRP: identify a single reason a class may change and extract other responsibilities.
OCP: add new behavior via new implementations of an abstraction rather than editing existing logic.
Practical refactor: interface-based design and a small orchestrator or service.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this lesson

narration.text: By the end of this lesson you will understand where SOLID fits into everyday C# design and be able to apply two principles immediately. First, you'll learn to recognize and apply the Single Responsibility Principle: separate data, persistence, validation, and messaging into focused components so a single change affects only a single module. For example, moving SaveToDatabase out of a User class into a repository reduces the chance that database changes break validation or email code. Second, you'll learn the Open/Closed Principle: design code that is closed to modification but open to extension. You'll practice this by using interfaces or strategies so new behavior can be added with a new class without modifying existing code. This reduces regressions in proven code. Finally, you'll gain techniques to spot violations and practical refactors that replace conditionals with polymorphism. These skills make C# projects easier to test, safer to evolve, and clearer for new team members.

screens.title: What is SRP?
screens.subtitle: A precise definition and why 'one reason to change' matters

narration.text: The Single Responsibility Principle states that a class should have only one reason to change. That means its public surface—methods and properties—should serve a single cohesive purpose. A useful mental model is: group together behavior that changes for the same reason. For example, data shape changes are one reason, persistence changes another, and communication or email formatting a third. If a single class mixes these concerns, a change in one area can cause a chain of edits and hidden regressions in unrelated behavior. A common misconception is equating SRP with 'one method per class'. That is wrong. A class may expose multiple methods as long as they contribute to the same responsibility. Concrete example: a User class that contains SaveToDatabase, SendWelcomeEmail, and IsValid violates SRP because database, email, and validation are separate responsibilities. The safer design is to keep a plain User data class and extract repository, email service, and validator interfaces. This yields classes that are easier to test in isolation, and when requirements change you change only the class responsible for that concern. Ask yourself: when this class needs to change, is it for one clear reason?

keyIdea.title: SRP in one line
keyIdea.text: Design classes so each has a single, well-defined reason to change; group methods by shared responsibility.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › What is SRP?
Definition

Single Responsibility Principle

A class should have one reason to change. Group methods that change together into the same class.

Misconceptions
  • A class with many methods is not automatically a SRP violation if methods share the same responsibility.
  • Over-extraction creates noise; apply SRP where responsibilities are truly distinct.
Key Takeaway

Isolate reasons to change. Extract responsibilities into clear interfaces and classes for safer changes.

Violation Example
// Violates SRP
public class User // Violates SRP
{
  public int Id { get; set; }
  public string Name { get; set; }
  public string Email { get; set; }

  public void SaveToDatabase()
  {
    Console.WriteLine($"Saving user {Name} to database...");
    // ... database persistence logic ...
  }

  public void SendWelcomeEmail()
  {
    Console.WriteLine($"Sending welcome email to {Email}...");
    // ... email sending logic ...
  }

  public bool IsValid()
  {
    // ... validation logic ...
    return !string.IsNullOrEmpty(Name) && !string.IsNullOrEmpty(Email);
  }
}
Concrete refactor
Extract IUserRepository, IEmailService, and IUserValidator. Keep User as a plain data holder and orchestrate operations in UserService.

screens.title: SRP Refactor — Split responsibilities
screens.subtitle: Extracting repositories, validators, and email services in C#

narration.text: Refactoring toward SRP involves identifying distinct responsibilities and moving each into a focused class or interface. Start by asking: what are the reasons this class might change? In the User example, reasons are persistence, email, and validation. The refactor pattern is straightforward: leave the data class, create interfaces for each external concern, and implement concrete classes that fulfill those contracts. For example, define IUserRepository with a Save method and implement SqlUserRepository. Create IEmailService and implement SmtpEmailService. Create IUserValidator and implement BasicUserValidator. Then introduce a UserService that composes those interfaces. This composition isolates changes: swapping the email provider or changing validation rules affects only the corresponding implementation. A common pitfall is over-abstracting everything immediately: prefer refactoring where responsibilities are likely to change. Another pitfall is leaking persistence logic back into the data model. A concrete example shows how RegisterUser uses the validator, repository, and email service in sequence. After the refactor, unit testing becomes easier because you can supply test doubles for each interface. How will you identify the next class to extract in your codebase? SRP Refactor — Split responsibilities means extract distinct responsibilities into interfaces and implement them in focused classes; orchestrate via a service.. In practical terms, extracting repositories, validators, and email services in c#. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Refactor pattern
keyIdea.text: Extract distinct responsibilities into interfaces and implement them in focused classes; orchestrate via a service.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › SRP Refactor
Refactor steps
  1. Identify distinct reasons to change—persistence, validation, messaging.
  2. Define small interfaces for each responsibility.
  3. Implement concrete classes and inject them into a service.
  4. Keep the data class pure and orchestrate behavior in the service.
Why this helps
Each implementation can change independently. Unit tests can replace collaborators with test doubles, and teams can work on different concerns without stepping on each other's code.
Code
public class User
{
  public int Id { get; set; }
  public string Name { get; set; }
  public string Email { get; set; }
}

public interface IUserRepository
{
  void Save(User user);
}

public class SqlUserRepository : IUserRepository
{
  public void Save(User user)
  {
    Console.WriteLine($"Saving user {user.Name} to SQL database...");
    // ... SQL database persistence logic ...
  }
}

public interface IEmailService
{
  void SendWelcomeEmail(User user);
}

public class SmtpEmailService : IEmailService
{
  public void SendWelcomeEmail(User user)
  {
    Console.WriteLine($"Sending welcome email to {user.Email} via SMTP...");
    // ... actual email sending logic ...
  }
}

public interface IUserValidator
{
  bool Validate(User user);
}

public class BasicUserValidator : IUserValidator
{
  public bool Validate(User user)
  {
    Console.WriteLine($"Validating user {user.Name}...");
    return !string.IsNullOrEmpty(user.Name) && !string.IsNullOrEmpty(user.Email);
  }
}

public class UserService
{
  private readonly IUserRepository _userRepository;
  private readonly IEmailService _emailService;
  private readonly IUserValidator _userValidator;

  public UserService(IUserRepository userRepository, IEmailService emailService, IUserValidator userValidator)
  {
    _userRepository = userRepository;
    _emailService = emailService;
    _userValidator = userValidator;
  }

  public void RegisterUser(User user)
  {
    if (!_userValidator.Validate(user))
    {
      Console.WriteLine("User validation failed.");
      return;
    }
    _userRepository.Save(user);
    _emailService.SendWelcomeEmail(user);
    Console.WriteLine($"User {user.Name} registered successfully.");
  }
}
Example orchestration keeps changes localized to repository, email service, or validator.

screens.title: What is OCP?
screens.subtitle: Open for extension, closed for modification explained

narration.text: The Open/Closed Principle says software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification. That means you should be able to add new behavior without changing the code that is already tested and working. In practical terms, achieve this by depending on abstractions—interfaces or abstract classes—so the client code works with a stable contract. New behaviors are added by creating new implementations of that contract. A common misconception is that OCP requires every class to be eternally extensible. That leads to over-abstraction. Instead, apply OCP where future variants are likely. A concrete violation shows a DiscountCalculator with if/else checks on product category. Every time a new category arrives you must modify the method. The refactor replaces the branching with an IDiscountStrategy interface and multiple strategies that the FlexibleDiscountCalculator accepts. This keeps the calculator stable while allowing new discount types to be added without touching the calculator code. Where would you apply OCP in your project without over-engineering? What is OCP? means prefer abstractions and new implementations to changing existing, tested code when adding behavior.. In practical terms, open for extension, closed for modification explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: OCP in practice
keyIdea.text: Prefer abstractions and new implementations to changing existing, tested code when adding behavior.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › What is OCP?
Definition

Open/Closed Principle

Design classes and modules so they can be extended without modifying existing code. Use abstractions and polymorphism to add behavior.

Practical guidance
  • Prefer adding a new implementation of an interface over changing an existing class.
  • Introduce extension points only where future change is expected; avoid over-abstraction.
Violation Example
public class Product
{
  public string Name { get; set; }
  public decimal Price { get; set; }
  public string Category { get; set; } // e.g., "Electronics", "Books"
}

public class DiscountCalculator // Violates OCP
{
  public decimal CalculateDiscount(Product product)
  {
    decimal discount = 0;
    if (product.Category == "Electronics")
    {
      discount = product.Price * 0.10m; // 10% off electronics
    }
    else if (product.Category == "Books")
    {
      discount = product.Price * 0.15m; // 15% off books
    }
    return discount;
  }
}
Adding a new category forces modification. OCP refactors introduce a strategy interface instead.

screens.title: OCP Refactor — Strategy pattern in C#
screens.subtitle: Introduce IDiscountStrategy and a flexible calculator

narration.text: To follow OCP, refactor conditional logic into a set of strategy implementations. Define an IDiscountStrategy interface with a CalculateDiscount method. Implement concrete strategies for electronics, books, and future categories. Then make the calculator accept an enumerable of IDiscountStrategy instances and iterate them to compute the total discount. This way, adding a new discount type is a matter of creating a new strategy class and registering it with the calculator, not editing the calculator itself. A common misconception is thinking the calculator must know how to choose strategies; instead, the calculator treats strategies as collaborators and trusts them to return zero when they don't apply. This allows composition: multiple strategies can contribute. A practical note: using dependency injection to supply strategies simplifies registration and testing. The refactor reduces risk because the calculator's behavior is stable while the system grows. Where in your codebase are there long if/else chains that could be replaced with small strategy classes? OCP Refactor — Strategy pattern in C# means replace branching with strategy implementations that can be added without changing the consumer code.. In practical terms, introduce idiscountstrategy and a flexible calculator. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Strategy for OCP
keyIdea.text: Replace branching with strategy implementations that can be added without changing the consumer code.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › OCP Refactor — Strategy
Architecture

IDiscountStrategy → FlexibleDiscountCalculator

Define a small interface for discount behavior and add implementations per category. The calculator remains unchanged as new strategies are added.

Pros
  • Safe extension without editing the calculator
  • Small testable strategy classes
Caveats
  • Avoid creating strategies for behavior that will never change
  • Prefer simple strategies that return zero when not applicable
Sample
public interface IDiscountStrategy
{
  decimal CalculateDiscount(Product product);
}

public class ElectronicsDiscountStrategy : IDiscountStrategy
{
  public decimal CalculateDiscount(Product product)
  {
    return product.Category == "Electronics" ? product.Price * 0.10m : 0;
  }
}

public class BooksDiscountStrategy : IDiscountStrategy
{
  public decimal CalculateDiscount(Product product)
  {
    return product.Category == "Books" ? product.Price * 0.15m : 0;
  }
}

public class FlexibleDiscountCalculator
{
  private readonly IEnumerable _discountStrategies;

  public FlexibleDiscountCalculator(IEnumerable discountStrategies)
  {
    _discountStrategies = discountStrategies;
  }

  public decimal GetTotalDiscount(Product product)
  {
    decimal totalDiscount = 0;
    foreach (var strategy in _discountStrategies)
    {
      totalDiscount += strategy.CalculateDiscount(product);
    }
    return totalDiscount;
  }
}
Register strategies with your DI container to add new discount types cleanly.

screens.title: DocumentSaver — From violation to OCP
screens.subtitle: Starter code, why it violates OCP, and the refactor plan

narration.text: The hands-on activity centers on a DocumentSaver that currently decides how to save documents based on a type parameter. This design violates OCP because adding a new storage option requires editing the SaveDocument method. The starter code shows a DocumentProcessor with branches for File and Cloud storage. Your refactor will introduce an IDocumentSaver interface, modify FileDocumentSaver to implement it, and add a CloudDocumentSaver stub that also implements the interface. Then change the client to depend on IDocumentSaver implementations rather than a type string. This demonstrates OCP: the processor’s client code does not change when you add new savers. A useful exercise is to simulate cloud saving with Console. WriteLine so behavior is visible in a console demo. Common mistakes include leaving the type switch in place or moving the switch to another class instead of replacing it with polymorphism. After the refactor, test the client by supplying different IDocumentSaver implementations from the Main method to prove the client code remains unchanged. content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › DocumentSaver Activity
Scenario

Refactor for OCP

You have a DocumentProcessor that selects a save strategy by type. The team expects cloud storage later. Refactor to open for extension and closed for modification.

Steps to refactor
  1. Define IDocumentSaver with a Save method.
  2. Make FileDocumentSaver implement IDocumentSaver.
  3. Create CloudDocumentSaver stub implementing IDocumentSaver.
  4. Change the client to accept IDocumentSaver instances, not a type string.
Starter (violating) code
// Program.cs
using System;
using System.IO;

public class Document
{
  public string Title { get; set; }
  public string Content { get; set; }
}

// Initial design - violates OCP if we add more saving types directly here
public class DocumentProcessor // This class will need modification if new saving methods are added
{
  public void SaveDocument(Document doc, string type, string destination)
  {
    if (type == "File")
    {
      Console.WriteLine($"Saving document '{doc.Title}' to local file: {destination}");
      File.WriteAllText(destination, doc.Content);
    }
    else if (type == "Cloud")
    {
      Console.WriteLine($"Saving document '{doc.Title}' to cloud storage: {destination}");
      // Imagine cloud specific API calls here
    }
    // PROBLEM: Adding "Database" saving would require modifying this method.
  }
}
Refactor by introducing IDocumentSaver and replacing conditional dispatch with DI-managed implementations.

screens.title: SRP vs OCP — When to apply each
screens.subtitle: How SRP and OCP complement each other and where they differ

narration.text: SRP and OCP address different aspects of change. SRP focuses on minimizing reasons for change inside a single module by grouping like responsibilities. It answers the question: what makes this class change? OCP focuses on how to accommodate new behavior without touching proven code; it answers the question: how can we add this variant without modifying the existing implementation? They complement each other: SRP helps keep modules small and focused, and OCP helps those modules remain stable while the system grows. A common mistake is to apply OCP everywhere, creating many tiny interfaces that never change. Use OCP where you expect new variants. Another mistake is to conflate SRP with having many tiny classes; instead, ensure each class represents a meaningful responsibility. Concrete example: use SRP to extract a repository and an email service, then use OCP on your discount calculator so you can add new discount types. The practical test is whether adding a new feature requires editing existing tests and code or only requires adding a new, focused implementation. SRP vs OCP — When to apply each means use srp to isolate responsibilities and ocp to allow new variants; apply both judiciously where change is expected.. In practical terms, how srp and ocp complement each other and where they differ. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: How they work together
keyIdea.text: Use SRP to isolate responsibilities and OCP to allow new variants; apply both judiciously where change is expected.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › SRP vs OCP

Comparison

SRP narrows the focus of a class. OCP provides extension points so new features don't require modifying tested code. Both reduce coupling, but they attack different dimensions of change.

SRP
Isolate responsibilities. Extract repositories, validators, and messaging to avoid multiple reasons to change a class.
OCP
Provide abstractions and add new implementations rather than editing the consumer of the abstraction.
Decision guide
Ask: is this change a new kind of behavior or a change in the existing responsibility? New kinds -> apply OCP. Multiple responsibilities inside one class -> apply SRP.
Concrete example
If you extract the repository from a User class (SRP), you can then implement multiple repositories for SQL, NoSQL, or in-memory testing. If the decision logic for discounts is replaced by strategies (OCP), adding a new discount only requires a new strategy class.
Key Takeaway

SRP clarifies responsibilities; OCP provides clean extension points. Use both to make code safer to change.

screens.title: Refactoring checklist
screens.subtitle: A repeatable process for SRP and OCP refactors

narration.text: When you refactor for SRP and OCP, follow a clear checklist so changes are safe and incremental. First, write or confirm existing unit tests that cover current behavior. Second, identify a single responsibility to extract by asking why code would change. Third, create a small interface for that responsibility and implement a concrete class. Fourth, inject the new dependency into callers and update the callers to use the abstraction. Fifth, run tests and add tests for the new implementation. For OCP refactors that replace branching logic, identify the branching points and replace them with a strategy interface and implementations. Register strategies with your dependency injection container or pass them explicitly to the calculator. A common pitfall is changing too much at once. Do the smallest safe refactor and keep the consumer code working between steps. This incremental approach reduces the chance of regressions and keeps the codebase in a deployable state during the refactor. Refactoring checklist means refactor safely: test, extract interface, implement, inject, and verify. do small increments to avoid regressions.. In practical terms, a repeatable process for srp and ocp refactors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Checklist
keyIdea.text: Refactor safely: test, extract interface, implement, inject, and verify. Do small increments to avoid regressions.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Refactoring Checklist

Safe refactor process

1. Ensure tests
Have tests that capture current behavior before changing implementation.
2. Identify one responsibility
Find the smallest responsibility that deserves its own interface or class.
3. Extract interface and implementation
Create a focused interface and a concrete implementation for the current behavior.
4. Inject and adapt callers
Wire the implementation into callers via constructor injection or explicit parameters.
5. Verify and iterate
Run tests, add tests for the new implementation, and proceed incrementally.
Common mistakes
  • Changing multiple responsibilities at once.
  • Over-abstracting code that will not change.
  • Removing integration tests during the refactor.

screens.title: Quick assessment and misconceptions
screens.subtitle: Questions to test design intuition and common traps

narration.text: Testing your intuition helps solidify these principles. Consider a NotificationSender that switches on a type string to send email, SMS, or push. Which principle is violated? That's OCP, because adding a new notification type requires modifying the method. Next, imagine a CustomerManager that creates customers, validates input, and generates PDF invoices. Which principle is violated? That's SRP, because it has multiple reasons to change. A common trap is to refactor by moving conditionals into another class without introducing an abstraction. That only moves coupling; it doesn't provide extension points. Another trap is prematurely introducing interfaces for every small behavior. Interfaces are valuable when variants are expected. For practice, take a small class in your own code: list the reasons it might change, then pick one reason and sketch an interface for it. Does adding a new behavior require editing the class after your change? If yes, consider a different refactor. Which class from your codebase will you review next? Quick assessment and misconceptions means ask what reasons a class has to change and whether new behavior requires editing existing code; these are the tests for srp and ocp.. In practical terms, questions to test design intuition and common traps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: When not to over-apply
screens.subtitle: Avoiding premature abstraction and noisy interfaces

narration.text: While SRP and OCP are powerful, overusing them creates unnecessary complexity. Premature abstraction—introducing interfaces for every small method—makes code harder to navigate and increases the number of types a newcomer must understand. A better rule is: apply SRP and OCP where you have a clear, anticipated need. If a behavior is unlikely to vary, keep it concrete. If you find many small interfaces with only one implementation and no anticipated variants, reconsider. Instead, prefer internal refactors such as extracting a private method or an internal helper class until a second implementation becomes necessary. Another useful practice is to refactor on the next-change basis: wait until a new requirement or bug makes it clear that separation will pay off. This balances simplicity with flexibility. Ask yourself: will another implementation appear in the near future, or am I isolating code for hypothetical change? That question helps avoid unnecessary complexity while preserving the benefits of SRP and OCP where they matter. When not to over-apply means prefer refactoring when change is real. avoid many tiny interfaces unless you expect multiple implementations.. In practical terms, avoiding premature abstraction and noisy interfaces. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practical balance
keyIdea.text: Prefer refactoring when change is real. Avoid many tiny interfaces unless you expect multiple implementations.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › When Not to Over-Apply

Avoid premature abstraction

Create abstractions when you have reason to expect multiple implementations. Otherwise, prefer local refactors and keep the design simple.

Rule of thumb
Introduce an interface when you need to mock, replace, or extend behavior. Delay until a second implementation or clear requirement appears.
Incremental refactor
Make small, reversible changes and run tests frequently. If a second implementation appears later, extract the interface then.
Checklist
  • Is a second implementation likely?
  • Will this simplify testing or composition?
  • Can we refactor incrementally?

narration.text: Let's summarize the most important points. First: Single Responsibility Principle — a class should have one reason to change; group methods by a shared responsibility and extract others into focused classes. Second: Open/Closed Principle — prefer adding new implementations of an abstraction rather than editing existing, tested code. Use strategies or interfaces to extend behavior safely. Third: Abstraction and polymorphism are the tools you will use: interfaces and small classes allow composition and testing. Remember to apply these principles pragmatically: avoid premature abstraction, refactor incrementally, and always keep tests in place while changing code. These reminders should help you recognize violations and pick the appropriate refactor pattern in your day-to-day C# development. SRP
Keep a single responsibility per class to limit reasons for change.
OCP
Add new functionality via new implementations rather than editing stable code.
Abstraction
Interfaces and small implementations are the mechanisms to achieve SRP and OCP.
Summary

Apply SRP to isolate reasons to change and OCP to add behavior via extension points; do so pragmatically and incrementally.

screens.title: Three quick reminders
screens.subtitle: Short memory aids for daily coding

narration.text: Keep three short reminders in mind as you write and refactor code. First, ask 'what is the reason this class will change?' If multiple reasons exist, split responsibilities. Second, when you need new behavior, ask 'can I add a new implementation instead of editing this class?' If yes, apply OCP via an interface or strategy. Third, prefer small, testable components and incremental refactors rather than large rewrites. These reminders guide daily decisions and reduce future technical debt. Before ending the session, choose one small class in your code and apply the checklist: tests, one responsibility extraction, inject, verify. That short loop reinforces the habit of thoughtful, maintainable design. Ask why it changes
If more than one reason, extract responsibilities.
Prefer extension
Add new types via interfaces, not edits of tested code.
Refactor incrementally
Make small changes with tests to avoid regressions.
Final takeaway

Small, deliberate refactors guided by SRP and OCP produce code that stands the test of change.
